title: Conditionals: zero to third
tagline: Four ways to talk about if: facts, real futures, unreal presents and unreal pasts.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations
Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze (unless / provided / in case)
Speaking Part 3 — negotiating options with a partner
why: Every conditional answers the same question — what happens if something else happens? — but the four types are not interchangeable: mixing them up turns a general rule into an impossible fantasy, or a real plan into pure speculation. B2 First tests the whole system, from the linking words that replace if to the exact verb forms each type needs.

diagrams.title: The four conditionals at a glance

rows.label: Zero
cells: a general truth or a rule, true every time

rows.label: First
cells: a real possibility in the future

rows.label: Second
cells: an unreal or unlikely present or future

rows.label: Third
cells: an unreal past — it didn't happen

diagrams.title: How far from reality?

marks.label: If you train harder, you'll make the team.
If I had more free time, I would learn guitar.
If I had practised, I would have passed the audition.

diagrams.caption: The further the condition is from real life, the further the verb forms move from the present simple.

branches.label: unless (= if … not)
items: Unless you leave now, you'll miss the bus.
We won't go unless the rain stops.

branches.label: as long as / provided (that)
items: You can borrow my notes as long as you return them.
Provided that you finish on time, it's fine.

branches.label: even if
items: Even if it rains, the match will go ahead.
Even if she apologises, I won't forgive her that easily.

branches.label: in case
items: Take an umbrella in case it rains later.
I'll save you a seat in case you're late.

head: Type
Pattern
Example
Note
rows: If you heat ice, it melts.
if and when are interchangeable here
If Sofia finishes early, she'll help us.
If it rains, the trip might be cancelled.
If I were you, I would ask Miss Vega.
were for all persons in formal or careful English
If we practised more, we could win the tournament.
if + past perfect, would have + participle
If they had left earlier, they would have caught the train.
the moment for the condition has already passed

use.point: Zero conditional: facts, rules and things that are always true

examples.text: If the temperature drops below zero in the Andes, water freezes overnight.
If a student arrives after the bell, the teacher marks them late.

use.point: First conditional: real, likely situations in the future

examples.text: If Liam finishes his project tonight, he 'll present it tomorrow.
Unless Nadia practises every day, she won't be ready for the concert.
If the weather stays like this, the match might be cancelled.
examples.note: might = alternative to will, less certain

use.point: Second conditional: unreal or unlikely situations now or in the future

examples.text: If I were the head boy, I would change the school lunch menu.
examples.note: were for all persons; a hypothetical role

examples.text: If Mateo had more time, he could join the robotics team.
If people cared more about the coastline, there wouldn't be so much plastic on the beach.
examples.note: a present wish about how things are

use.point: Third conditional: unreal situations in the past — things that didn't happen

examples.text: If Sofia had checked the timetable, she wouldn't have missed the exam.
examples.note: a past mistake with a past consequence

examples.text: Provided that the coach had picked a stronger squad, they might have won the final.
examples.note: provided that in a formal, hypothetical past sentence

watch_out.wrong: If it will rain, we'll stay inside.
watch_out.why: No will in the if-clause of a first conditional, even though the meaning is about the future.

watch_out.wrong: If I was you, I would talk to Miss Vega.
watch_out.right: If I were you, I would talk to Miss Vega.
watch_out.why: Were is the expected form for all persons in the second conditional, especially in if I were you.

watch_out.wrong: Unless you don't hurry, we'll be late.
watch_out.why: Unless already means if not, so a second negative makes the sentence say the opposite of what you mean.

watch_out.wrong: If they would have trained harder, they would have won.
watch_out.right: If they had trained harder, they would have won.
watch_out.why: No would in the if-clause of a third conditional — it takes the past perfect.

watch_out.wrong: Take a jacket if it gets cold later.
watch_out.right: Take a jacket in case it gets cold later.
watch_out.why: In case means as a precaution, before something happens; if describes a direct condition and result.

watch_out.wrong: I'll lend you my notes as long as you will return them.
watch_out.right: I'll lend you my notes as long as you return them.
watch_out.why: After as long as and provided that, use the present simple, not will, even for a future meaning.

dialogue.title: Planning the trip to Cusco
dialogue.context: Mateo, Sofia and Nadia are deciding whether their class trip to Cusco will still go ahead, with Miss Vega checking the details.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: If the forms aren't in by Friday, the trip gets cancelled automatically. That's the school rule.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Then we need everyone's signature today. Unless we collect them all, Miss Vega won't confirm the bus.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: I'll ask Liam now. If he signs before lunch, we'll have every form.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good. And provided that the weather forecast stays good, we'll leave at six on Saturday.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Even if it rains a little, we'd still go, right? It's the Andes, after all.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: A little rain, yes. But if there were a storm warning, we would postpone it — safety first.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Makes sense. Last year, if we had checked the forecast properly, we wouldn't have got stuck in Ollantaytambo.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: True. I'm bringing an extra jumper this time, just in case it's cold at altitude.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Smart. If I were more organised, I would have packed already, like you two.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: There's still time. Now go and find Liam before that deadline.

items.why: a scientific fact → zero conditional, present simple

items.sentence: ___ you finish the essay tonight, we can check it together tomorrow.
If I ___ the captain, I would choose a completely different tactic.
items.why: second conditional, unreal present → were for all persons

items.sentence: They wouldn't have missed the flight if they ___ earlier.
items.why: third conditional, unreal past → past perfect in the if-clause

items.sentence: ___ it rains during the match, we'll still play — the pitch drains quickly.
items.why: the result happens despite the condition → even if

items.sentence: Bring your student card ___ they ask for identification at the museum.
items.why: a precaution before something might happen → in case

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with the correct form of the verb in brackets.

items.sentence: If the museum ___ (be) closed on Mondays, we'll go on Tuesday instead.
If I ___ (have) a car, I would drive you to training every day.
Unless the coach ___ (change) his mind, Liam won't start the final.
If Nadia ___ (not/practise) so hard last year, she wouldn't have made the orchestra.
Provided that you ___ (return) the equipment by Friday, there's no fine.
If people ___ (recycle) more, there would be far less rubbish on the coast.
If she ___ (ask) for help sooner, the project might have gone more smoothly.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first. Use the word given. Do not change it. Use between two and five words.

items.first: If you don't hand in the permission form, you won't be allowed on the trip.
items.second_start: You won't be allowed on the trip

items.first: I'm not the team captain, so I don't decide the tactics.
items.second_end: captain, I would decide the tactics.

items.first: They didn't book early, so they missed the discount.
items.second_end: early, they wouldn't have missed the discount.

It's possible that it will rain later, so take an umbrella.

summary: Zero conditional states a fact or a rule; first conditional describes a real possibility in the future.
Second conditional imagines an unreal or unlikely present, with were for every person; third conditional imagines an unreal past.
Unless, as long as, provided that, even if and in case all replace or add to if, each with its own logic.
The result clause is not always will or would — may, might and could soften the certainty.
Match the verb forms to how real or unreal the condition is: present simple → past simple → past perfect, moving further from reality.
